experience_text: When evaluating data retention policies, recognize that the mere presence of a disclosure provision does not necessarily imply a statement about data storage duration. Treat clauses that only address information sharing or user rights as insufficient evidence of data retention policies.

When a document describes a mechanism for collecting user information and its purpose, treat it as a description of how and why the service provider collects user information, even if the description is indirect or implicit.

When you see a clause describing how a service provider will inform users about changes to its privacy policy, do not assume it also describes how and why the provider collects user information. Treat these as distinct concepts and require explicit language about collection and use.

When a document describes using collected information for specific purposes, recognize that as an implicit description of how and why the service provider collects user information, even if it does not explicitly state the collection process or its legal basis.

When a document describes a user's choice to provide personal information for a specific service, recognize that this choice implies the service provider's collection and use of that information. Treat such descriptions as evidence of first-party collection and use.

When a document describes a user action that involves providing personal information, recognize that as a description of how and why the service provider collects user information, even if the user's action is framed as optional.

When a clause describes a specific action that involves collecting user information, recognize that it may implicitly describe how and why the service provider collects user information, even if it does not explicitly state the purpose.
When a document describes a privacy policy and the practices it entails, recognize that it implicitly addresses how and why user information is collected, even if it does not explicitly state so.

When you see a description of data collection methods and examples of data collected, treat it as a description of how and why user information is collected, even if the text does not explicitly state the purpose.

When a clause describes the collection of user information and its intended use, treat it as a description of how and why the information is collected, even if the language does not explicitly state 'why'. Recognize that the purpose of the collection can be inferred from the context.

When classifying clauses about information collection, recognize that sharing user information with third parties does not necessarily imply the service provider's own collection or use of that information. Treat clauses that only describe sharing or disclosure as distinct from those that describe collection or use.

When a document describes the collection of user information in the context of a specific transaction or service, recognize that as a description of how and why the information is collected, even if the language does not explicitly state 'we collect this information for this purpose'.

When you see a description of how user information is used to fulfill requests, improve services, or send promotional offers, recognize that as a collection and use of user information, even if the exact query keywords are not present.

When a document describes the collection of user information, even if it clarifies that personally identifiable information is not accessed, treat it as a description of how and why a service provider collects user information.

When you see a list of entities with whom personal information may be shared, do not assume this directly addresses how and why a service provider collects user information. Recognize that data sharing and data collection are distinct concepts.

When evaluating a clause's description of user information collection, recognize that third-party certifications and seals of approval do not necessarily imply a description of the service provider's own collection practices. Treat such certifications as evidence of compliance with external standards, rather than as a direct description of the service provider's actions.

When you see a document describing a procedure for opting out of data collection, do not assume it also explains the purpose of the data collection. Recognize that the 'why' of data collection may not be explicitly stated alongside the 'how'.

When you see a statement about not sharing information, recognize that it does not necessarily describe how and why the service provider collects user information, but rather how the information is used or shared after collection.

When you see a statement about not sharing or selling user information, recognize that it does not necessarily imply the collection or use of that information. Treat such statements as insufficient evidence for a yes answer unless accompanied by an explicit description of collection or use.

When a clause explicitly limits its scope to a specific demographic or jurisdiction, recognize that as a description of practices pertaining only to that group, even if the clause's main topic is a general disclosure requirement.

When a clause explicitly limits its scope to a specific geographic or demographic group, treat it as describing practices that pertain only to that group, even if the query's example groups are not mentioned.

When a clause mentions a specific demographic in the context of a warning or guidance, treat it as describing practices that pertain to that group, even if the clause does not explicitly restrict its scope to that group.

When you see a clause describing data collection, do not assume it implies a method for informing users about changes to the policy. Recognize that data collection and user notification are distinct concepts.

When you see a clause describing how user information is collected, used, or disclosed, do not assume it also describes sharing with or collection by third parties unless explicitly stated. Treat general statements about information handling as insufficient evidence for third-party sharing or collection.

When you see a document that only describes the process of collecting user information, but does not explicitly mention user access, editing, or deletion rights, answer No. Recognize that the mere collection of personal data does not necessarily imply user control over that data.

When you see a list of accessible information, recognize that it does not necessarily imply the ability to edit or delete that information. Treat access separately from edit and deletion capabilities.

When you see a clause describing access to a database for official investigations or legal proceedings, do not assume it implies user access, editing, or deletion rights. Treat such language as describing a separate, unrelated process.

When you see a statement of consent, do not assume it implies user control options. Recognize that consent and control are distinct concepts, and require explicit language to indicate choices available to users.
